newsitem.title: UK: FULL TEXT-UK budget changes to capital allowances.
newsitem.headline: FULL TEXT-UK budget changes to capital allowances.

text.p: Following is the full text of a UK Treasury news release on changes to capital allowances announced in Britain's budget on Wednesday:
HIGHER CAPITAL ALLOWANCES FOR SMALL AND MEDIUM-SIZED BUSINESSES

Small and medium-sized businesses will benefit from a doubling of the rate of capital allowances for investment on machinery and plant in the next 12 months under proposals announced by the Chancellor today. More than 99 per cent of all businesses will qualify. The doubled allowances will help them to grow and to invest.

The new rules will apply to expenditure by these businesses on machinery and plant, other than cars and certain other assets, in the year ended 1 July 1998. The rate of capital allowances will be increased from 25 per cent to 50 per cent for allowances in the first year.
It is estimated that small and medium-sized businesses will pay 230 million Pounds less tax in the year 1998-99 and 170 million Pounds less tax in the year 1999-2000 as a result of this change.
DETAILS

1. At present, capital allowances are given on machinery and plant at 25 per cent a year on the reducing balance basis. This means that relief of 25 per cent of the cost is given for the year in which the equipment is bought, 25 per cent of the balance remaining is given for the following year and so on.

2. Capital allowances are given at six per cent a year on machinery and plant with an expected working life of 25 years or more ("long life assets"). But this does not generally apply to businesses spending less than 100,000 Pounds a year on long life assets which excludes nearly all small and medium-sized businesses.

3. Under the Budget proposals, expenditure on machinery or plant incurred during the 12 months ended 1 July 1998 by small and medium-sized businesses will qualify for a first-year allowance at double the normal rate of writing-down allowance, that is 50 per cent in general or 12 per cent where, exceptionally, the long life asset rules apply.

4. The new rate will apply to the first year for which allowances are due. For subsequent years, allowances will be due on the balance remaining at 25 per cent, or 6 per cent where, exceptionally, the long life asset rules apply, as before.

5. It is estimated that small and medium-sized businesses will pay 230 million Pounds less tax in the year 1998-99 and 170 million Pounds less tax in the year 1999-2000 as a result of this change. There will be some increase in their tax bills in later years as the balance of unrelieved expenditure carried forward will be reduced by the higher allowances.
They will however gain additional allowances on increases in investment and the cash flow benefit of earlier allowances on all their investment in the next 12 months.

Businesses that qualify 6. The new rate will apply to businesses which are small or medium-sized using the Companies Act definitions. These are broadly that it satisfies two of the following conditions:
- turnover not more than 11.2 million Pounds, - assets not more than 5.6 million Pounds, and - not more than 250 employees.

or was small or medium-sized for the previous year. 7. In the case of companies, the company must be small or medium-sized for the year in which the expenditure is incurred to qualify for the new rate. If the company is a member of a group, the group must be small or medium-sized.
8. The new rate will also apply to businesses carried on by individuals and partnerships made up of individuals provided the business would qualify if it were carried on by a company.
Exclusions from the new rate
9. The new rate will not apply to expenditure on machinery and plant for leasing, cars, sea-going ships and railway assets.

10. The new rate will not apply to expenditure which is excluded from the rules on long life assets under the transitional rules, broadly long life assets bought on or after 26 November 1996 under a contract entered into before that date.
NOTES FOR EDITORS

1. Capital allowances allow the cost of capital assets to be written off against the taxable profits. They take the place of depreciation charged in the commercial accounts, which is not allowable for tax.

2. First year allowances on machinery and plant were phased out in the 1984 business tax reforms. They were reintroduced temporarily for expenditure incurred during the 12 months ended 31 October 1993.
